notes.meaning: John receives a measuring rod shaped like a staff and is told to measure God's temple, its altar, and the people worshiping inside. Measuring shows that God knows, claims, and protects His own people during times of trouble. Believers are assured that God keeps careful watch over their worship and safety.

differ.view: The temple refers to a literal physical Jewish temple that will be rebuilt in Jerusalem before the return of Christ.
The temple is a symbol for the true, spiritual church which God protects from spiritual harm.

notes.meaning: John is instructed to leave out the courtyard outside the temple because the nations will trample the holy city for forty-two months. Leaving out this open court means that worldly or unfaithful worshipers will not receive God's special protection. The forty-two months represents a limited season of hardship that God allows and firmly controls.

differ.view: The forty-two months is a literal period of three and a half years of intense persecution near the very end of history.
The forty-two months is a symbolic number representing the entire church age between Christ's first and second comings.

notes.meaning: God promises to send two witnesses who will preach for 1,260 days dressed in sackcloth, which is rough cloth worn in times of grief. The sackcloth shows their deep sorrow over the world's rebellion against God. Having two messengers confirms that their warning of judgment is reliable and true under God's law.

differ.view: The two witnesses are two literal future men who will prophesy in Jerusalem, possibly Moses and Elijah or prophets like them.
The two witnesses symbolize the whole faithful church fulfilling its calling to bear witness to Jesus in the world.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Many early church fathers identified the two witnesses as Enoch and Elijah because neither of those men died a physical death in the Old Testament.

notes.meaning: These witnesses are identified as the two olive trees and two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth. This imagery comes from the prophet Zechariah, where olive trees supply oil to keep lamps burning with holy light. In the same way, the Holy Spirit constantly supplies these witnesses with spiritual grace and power to shine for God.

Anyone who tries to harm the two witnesses is consumed by fire coming from their mouths. This protective fire shows that God's spoken judgment will directly destroy anyone seeking to silence His messengers. God shields His servants completely so that no one can end their mission before their work is done.

The witnesses are given power to lock up the sky so that no rain falls, to turn waters into blood, and to strike the earth with plagues. These miracles recall Elijah, who prayed for drought, and Moses, who brought plagues upon Egypt. These signs prove that the messengers preach with genuine divine authority.

When the witnesses finish their testimony, a beast rising from the Abyss attacks, overpowers, and kills them. The Abyss refers to the demonic pit of darkness and imprisonment. Evil is allowed to take their lives only after their appointed message is fully delivered.

The dead bodies of the witnesses are left lying in the street of the great city that is figuratively called Sodom and Egypt. This city is identified as the place where their Lord was crucified, pointing to Jerusalem and to worldly systems hostile to God. Leaving their bodies unburied was intended as the ultimate public insult and act of shame.

People from all tribes, languages, and nations gaze at the dead bodies for three and a half days while refusing them a grave. The enemies of God want the whole world to view the spectacle and witness their supposed defeat. This cruelty displays how fiercely the fallen world despises God's truth.

People across the earth rejoice over the dead prophets by celebrating and sending gifts to one another. They celebrate because the warnings and miracles of the witnesses had tormented their guilty consciences. Rejecting God's truth leads people to celebrate the destruction of what is good.

After three and a half days, God's breath of life enters the two witnesses, and they stand up on their feet. This miracle mirrors the vision of dry bones coming back to life in the book of Ezekiel. Those who watch them rise are instantly struck with deep terror as God displays His resurrecting power.

A loud voice from heaven summons the witnesses to come up, and they rise into heaven in a cloud before the eyes of their enemies. Their ascension echoes the way Jesus was taken up into the clouds after His resurrection. God openly vindicates His servants and proves that death cannot defeat them.

A violent earthquake strikes the city at that very moment, bringing down a tenth of its buildings and killing seven thousand people. The survivors are terrified and give glory to the God of heaven. This judgment forces the remaining onlookers to acknowledge God's supreme authority.

The second woe comes to an end, and John warns that the third woe is arriving quickly. The second woe included the sixth trumpet judgment and the account of the two witnesses. Readers are urged to pay close attention as the final trumpet judgment prepares to sound.

The seventh angel sounds his trumpet, and loud voices in heaven proclaim that the kingdom of the world now belongs to the Lord and His Christ. This marks the glorious moment when God's eternal rule replaces all earthly empires. Believers take comfort in knowing that Christ's righteous reign will never end.

The twenty-four elders sitting on their thrones before God fall on their faces to worship Him. These elders represent the whole redeemed family of God from all generations. In the presence of Christ's triumph, they respond with humble adoration and wholehearted praise.

The elders give thanks to the Almighty Lord who is and who was, praising Him for taking up His supreme power and beginning His reign. They do not add "who is to come," because the promised day of His kingdom has now arrived. God's people rejoice that His sovereign rule has overcome every opposing force.

The nations raged against God, but now His righteous anger has come to judge the dead and set all things right. God promises to reward His faithful prophets, saints, and all who honor His name, while destroying those who corrupt the earth. This judgment assures believers that true justice will prevail.

God's heavenly temple opens up, revealing the ark of His covenant inside the most holy place. The ark was the sacred chest that symbolized God's holy presence and His faithful promises to His people. Lightning, thunder, and a great hailstorm show forth His majestic power and point toward the final judgments to come.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching often connects the heavenly ark to Mary, who bore Jesus within her, viewing this vision as leading directly into the woman clothed with the sun in chapter 12.
